# The course

## Two courses, one project {.smaller}

AEM 6991 (fall). You produce a *plan* — a question, a design, and
evidence that the data exists.

AEM 6992 (spring). You *execute* that plan.

The deliverable in December is a proposal somebody could hand to a team in
January.

::: {.notes}
Everything you commit to in the fall you live with in the spring. A
question that is vague in October is a disaster in March.
:::

## What this course is for {.smaller}

By December you should be able to:

- Find a question worth a semester, and say why it matters
- Design a study that could answer it — and name the assumption
  carrying it
- Prove the data exists, can be obtained, and measures what you need
- Say what you can and cannot claim, and defend that in a room
- Work in a team that delivers on time, with the work split fairly

::: {.notes}
These are the registrar's four outcomes for 6991 plus the two this
section adds — evidence sourcing, and design vocabulary. Do not read
them off. Say the fifth one is graded as hard as the rest, because the
course description calls teamwork a major component and every other
section treats it as goodwill.
:::

## What this is not {.smaller}

You are not writing a paper for a journal.

- No gap in the literature to fill
- No contribution to claim
- Nobody is going to referee this for *AJAE*

::: {.notes}
The single most common misunderstanding. Students hear "research design"
and reach for the genre they have seen in seminars. Kill it here.
:::

## What it is {.smaller}

> You are building the analysis a competent team would need before making a
> decision that costs real money.
>
> The standard for "competent" is the same standard a referee would apply.

Rigor and genre are different axes. The rigor bar does not move. The
genre does.

::: {.notes}
If the design would not survive a referee, it does not survive here. But
the audience is a decision-maker, not a discipline.

This also rescues the literature review from feeling academic: you read to
find out whether your question is already answered, not to find a gap.
:::

## What good work looks like {.smaller}

Two questions move a grade more than anything else.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Is the claim in the first sentence?

And could it come out the other way?
:::

Your proposal is graded against the headings it has to answer. They are on
the site, and we come back to them all term.

::: {.notes}
Do not read the thirteen headings out on day one — they have no project
yet and it lands as a wall. Point at the syllabus and move on.

The convention is shared across the 6991 sections: criteria are the
headings a paper must answer, not a points rubric.

Say the thing they will not expect: stating a limitation well EARNS marks.
Hiding one costs them. Most students arrive believing the opposite.

## Quizzes {.smaller}

Short, in class, and without warning. About six across the semester.

- Three questions, three minutes, on your own device
- On the lecture you are sitting in, not on a reading
- Tied to your NetID — it is also the attendance record
- The lowest is dropped, so an honest miss costs nothing

::: {.notes}
Say why they are unannounced: a quiz you can revise for is a reading
check, and a quiz you cannot is a reason to be here and paying
attention. That is the thing worth rewarding.

No quiz today. Say the mechanic and move on.
:::

## AI: permitted, disclosed, verified {.smaller}

Writing the code is no longer the scarce skill. Neither is drafting the
prose. Knowing what to ask for is. So is noticing when the answer is wrong.

From meeting 12 you work with real data through an assistant. What is
graded is the questions you ask and the checks you run, never code you
wrote.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
McKinsey now runs analyst interviews where you work a problem live on
their AI platform, and they score how you prompt it, how you catch it
being wrong, and how you turn that into a recommendation.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say plainly that policies differ across sections and that this one is
deliberately permissive. The McKinsey fact IS the reason, so do not rush
it. Employers put "skills using AI tools" FIRST on what they expect to
value in five years, while ranking it 14th today.

Do NOT bring the grim version into week 1 — entry-level postings down
35%, a third of employers already substituting AI. True, and it will
flatten the room. It belongs in meeting 14.
:::

## The one that will bite you {.smaller}

Ask an assistant for references on your topic. Right now.

Then open every single one.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
A fabricated citation in your literature review is an academic integrity
violation.

"The AI generated it" is not a defence. It is an admission that you
submitted something you never read.
:::

::: {.notes}
LIVE DEMO — 5 minutes, do not skip it. Take a topic from the room, ask an
assistant for five references with DOIs, then check them together on the
screen.

Expect a mix: some real, some plausible and wrong — real authors, real
journal, invented title or year. If everything comes back real, say so
honestly and try a narrower topic; the failure rate rises fast as the
topic narrows.

The lesson is not "AI is bad." It is that verification is the one step
you can never delegate, which is the same lesson as meeting 12.
:::

# Finding a question

## Where ideas come from {.smaller}

1. A gap in what is known
2. Extending or contesting a published result
3. An anomaly — something that should not be true
4. A decision somebody actually has to make
5. A dataset that exists and nobody has looked at properly

Route 5 is the most dangerous, and we come back to why.

::: {.notes}
Routes are where the idea comes from. That is not the same as what shape
it has to take — which is the next twenty minutes, and the part that
actually constrains you.
:::

## This part is the job {.smaller}

Most of your education has rewarded execution. Do the analysis well. Write
it up clearly.

This course rewards the part before that. Finding a question worth
answering is a separate skill. It is harder than executing one.

And it is the most enjoyable thing you will do all semester. Do not rush
it.

::: {.notes}
Say this slowly and mean it. Students arrive believing the creative part
is a preamble to the real work. It is the real work — 6992 is where they
execute, and a bad question executed beautifully is still a bad project.
:::

## Is there a method? {.smaller}

Partly. Two ideas have real evidence behind them.

Start from your means, not your goal. Experts do not pick a goal and
hunt for means. They start from what they have — who they are, what they
know, whom they know — and work forward.

Generate, then judge. Never both at once. Teams that evaluate while
brainstorming produce fewer ideas, and safer ones.

::: {.notes}
The first is effectuation, from Sarasvathy's think-aloud studies of expert
entrepreneurs. It is the licence for what happens this afternoon.

The second is why session B separates writing your interest down from
having somebody else judge it. Say that when you set it up.
:::

## What the last two cohorts did {.smaller}

2026

ESG strategy → return on equity · inventory turnover → performance ·
investor sentiment → S&P return · Wikipedia pageviews → stock returns ·
what drives engagement on TikTok

2023

Twitter sentiment → NFT returns · social media sentiment → stock return ·
weather → stock return · ESG score → annual return · organic food choices ·
sustainability and Gen Z purchasing

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Four of the five 2026 projects are the same project. What is it?
:::

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Do not answer it for them — someone will get there, and it
lands infinitely harder from a student than from me.

The answer: take a public signal anybody can download, regress a financial
outcome on it, report a coefficient. Free data, no design, no decision
attached.

Then the question that matters: WHY did that happen? Not laziness. The
data was free and available and the question got shaped to fit it. That is
anti-pattern 2, and it is the default unless you actively resist it.

Then the permission they need to hear: the most ambitious project anyone
remembers ran online experiments on brand recognition, then talked a soda
company into donating thousands of cans and ran a field experiment in
dining halls. Nine-month MPS team. No econometrics — nerve, and knowing it
was allowed. It is allowed.
:::

## Six anti-patterns {.smaller}

1. The topic with no question. "AI in finance."
2. The dataset in search of a question. You found a nice dataset and
   have been reverse-engineering a question onto it since.
3. The consulting deck. Secondary research with no empirical work of your own.
4. The unobtainable-data project. Beautiful design; requires
   proprietary data from a firm nobody on the team knows.
5. The dissertation. Correctly scoped for three years.
6. The already-answered question. This is what the literature review
   is *for*.

::: {.notes}
Number 2 is why this course is ordered question, then design, then data.
Teams who find data first rationalize a question around it, every time.

Number 4 has to die by meeting 12, in the outline's data section. Not in
January.
:::

## The feasibility filter {.smaller}

Four questions. A "no" on any one is fatal — and cheap to discover *now*.

1. Could a team of 3–5 execute this in one spring semester?
2. Can you name the specific dataset, who holds it, and how you get it
   — *checked, not assumed*?
3. Does the design produce an answer that could come out either way?
4. Would somebody actually act differently depending on the answer?

::: {.notes}
Question 2 is the one they will fudge. Push on "checked, not assumed" —
have you opened the page, found the access terms, seen the actual columns?

This filter is what session B runs on. Do not cut it.
:::

# Session B · Your interests

## What this hour is for {.smaller}

Teams do not exist yet. I form them from what you tell each other this
afternoon, and from the statement you write this week.

So the job is to get your interest into one sentence somebody else can
repeat back to you.

::: {.notes}
Say plainly that this is not a brainstorm and not an icebreaker. It is the
input to team formation, and the quality of what they write is the quality
of the teams they get.
:::

## Write your card {.smaller}

Three lines. Ten minutes. Your name at the top.

1. What you are interested in, in one sentence
2. One thing you bring that most people in this room do not — a job,
   an industry, a language, access to somebody
3. One person or organisation who would do something differently if
   they knew the answer

::: {.notes}
Line 3 is the one that does the work. If they cannot name anybody, the
interest is still a topic — say so, and say that is fine today.

Circulate. Read over shoulders. This is your first real signal for team
formation and it is better than the statements you get next week.
:::

## Now trade {.smaller}

Three rounds. Seven minutes each. New partner every round.

| | Your partner's job |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | Say your interest back to you in one sentence. You accept it or fix it |
| 2 | Name who would act on the answer |
| 3 | Name what you have that the room does not — and one person here you should talk to |

Your partner writes on your card and signs it.

::: {.notes}
Call time firmly at seven minutes. The rotation is the point — three
strangers reading the same sentence is what turns a topic into a question.

If the room is odd-numbered, join in yourself.
:::

## The wall {.smaller}

Every card goes up.

Five minutes to walk the room and put your initials on any card whose
question you would be glad to work on.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Initials mean *"I would work on this"* — not *"this is good"*.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say the framing BEFORE the vote, not after.

Then read out the three with the most initials. Do not read out the ones
with none — read the count if you must, never the name. An interest nobody
else picked is often the one with the least competition for it.

Collect every card. They are the artifact, and they are half of how you
form teams next week.
:::

Before you assume data has to be bought or scraped:

- The Cornell library's licensed holdings — more than most students

- Dewey, a commercial data marketplace the Johnson College subscribes

Register tonight at [app.deweydata.io](https://app.deweydata.io) with
your Cornell email — approval is a human step, so it takes days.

::: {.notes}
Five minutes at the end, on the projector, from YOUR account — students

Teams routinely propose buying data the College already has. Others drop a

:::

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

### The arc

AEM 6991 produces a *plan*; AEM 6992 *executes* it. The deliverable in
December is a proposal somebody could hand to a team in January.

### AI ground rules

Permitted by default, disclosure mandatory, verification graded. From
meeting 12 you work with real data through an assistant, and what is
graded is the questions you ask and the checks you run — never code you
wrote.

**Every reference gets opened.** A fabricated citation is an academic
integrity violation, and "the AI generated it" is an admission that you
submitted something you never read.

### What this is, and is not

You are not writing a paper for a journal — there is no gap to fill and no
contribution to claim. You are building the analysis a competent team would
need before making a decision that costs real money, and the standard for
"competent" is the same standard a referee would apply. Rigor and genre are
different axes: the rigor bar does not move, the genre does.

This is also why the literature matters without the project being a
literature project. You read to find out whether your question is already
answered, and how people have answered questions like it.

For context, MPS AEM class of 2025: 40% into finance, 21% marketing and
sales, 15% general management, 13% consulting, 6% data and analytics.
Essentially none into research.

### Where ideas come from

Five routes: a gap in what is known; extending or contesting a published
result; an anomaly; a decision somebody has to make; a dataset nobody has
looked at properly. The last is the most dangerous.

### Coming up with the idea is the job

Most of your education has rewarded execution. This course rewards the
part before it. A bad question executed beautifully is still a bad
project.

It is also the most enjoyable part of the work. Give it the time.

### Is there a method for having ideas?

Partly. Two of the popular answers have real evidence; most do not.

**Start from your means, not your goal.** This is
[effectuation](https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2001.4378020), from Saras Sarasvathy's think-aloud
studies of expert entrepreneurs. Experts do not pick a goal and search
for the means to reach it. They start from who they are, what they know
and whom they know, and work forward. Sarasvathy's phrase is that they
*make* opportunities rather than find them.

You have a Dewey account, a concentration and a team with particular
backgrounds. Working forward from those is not a lesser way of doing it.
It is what expertise looks like. What keeps it honest is the feasibility
filter — means-driven reasoning turns into anti-pattern 2 the moment you
stop being willing to walk away from the means.

**Generate, then judge. Never both at once.** Teams that evaluate while
brainstorming produce fewer ideas, and safer ones. Session B separates the
two on purpose: you write first, and only then does anyone judge it.

**Ask what job somebody is hiring the answer to do.**
[Jobs to be Done](https://hbr.org/2016/09/know-your-customers-jobs-to-be-done) reframes a question from "what does
this do" to "what is somebody trying to accomplish". That is feasibility
filter 4, arrived at from another direction. The reframing is useful; the
evidence behind it is thin.

**For research questions specifically**,
[Sandberg and Alvesson](https://doi.org/10.1177/1350508410372151) separate *gap-spotting* — finding
what the literature has not covered — from *problematization*, which
challenges an assumption the literature shares. Gap-spotting is easier
and produces most published work. Problematization produces the
interesting work and is riskier. For one semester, gap-spotting is
usually right. Knowing which you are doing is what stops you overclaiming.

A caution that applies here as everywhere in this course. **Being taught
in every business school is not evidence that something works.** Design
thinking as a branded five-step method, and lean startup, are widely
taught and lightly tested.

### The five archetypes

Every project should be able to say in one sentence which of these it is. A
project that cannot pick one is not yet a project.

| | Archetype | Question | Claim | Design | Fails when |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Evaluation | Did it work? | Causal, retrospective | DiD, event study, RD, IV | No credible comparison group |
| 2 | Preference & pricing | What would they choose and pay? | Causal, but elicited | Choice experiments, conjoint | Stated read as revealed |
| 3 | Prediction & risk | What happens next? | Predictive, *not causal* | Out-of-sample validation | Causal claims off a predictive model |
| 4 | Diagnosis & benchmarking | Where is the gap? | Descriptive | Decomposition, benchmarking | Description dressed as cause |
| 5 | Feasibility & landscape | Is this real? | Synthesis + original work | Market sizing, benchmarking | No empirical component |

Archetype 5 is approved only if it contains a specific, checkable empirical
question you answer with data you analyze yourselves.

### Six anti-patterns

The topic with no question; the dataset in search of a question; the
consulting deck; the unobtainable-data project; the dissertation; the
already-answered question.

### The feasibility filter

1. Could a team of 3–5 execute this in one spring semester?
2. Can you name the specific dataset, who holds it, and how you get it —
   checked, not assumed?
3. Does the design produce an answer that could come out either way?
4. Would somebody actually act differently depending on the answer?

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

### The literature workshop

You search for two reasons: to find out whether somebody has already
answered your question, and to see how people answer questions like it.

Start broad, then chase citations — one good recent paper gives you its
reference list and everything citing it since. Read abstract, then figures
and tables, then conclusion, then method. Business sources count; for most
archetypes they matter more than journals.

Screen with one line per paper: question, design, data, what they found,
why it matters to us. Five to eight rows is enough at this stage.

### What you already have access to

Before assuming data must be bought or scraped: the Cornell library's
licensed holdings, and **Dewey**, a commercial data marketplace the Johnson
College of Business subscribes to and which you can use at no cost. Teams
routinely propose buying data the College already has, or drop a good
question because they assumed the data was unreachable.

**Register at [app.deweydata.io](https://app.deweydata.io) with your
Cornell email**, in week 1. Your account sits pending until an
administrator approves it, so do not leave it until you need the data.

If you are stuck, there is a numbered list of leads under Resources —
[potential project ideas](../project-ideas.qmd). Treat it as a way to
get unstuck, not a menu. Nobody has ever written a good capstone from
somebody else's idea list.

Working backwards from a dataset is legitimate — it is route 5 — provided
you do it honestly: what could this answer, which of those would anybody act
on, and what does it not contain that you would need? The question still has
to survive the filter, and you are still allowed to walk away from the data.
Route 5 done badly is anti-pattern 2.

### Your interests

Teams do not exist yet. They are formed from what you tell each other this
afternoon and from the statement of interest you write this week.

Write a card: what you are interested in, in one sentence; one thing you
bring that most people in this room do not; and one person or organisation
who would do something differently if they knew the answer. The third line
is the one that does the work. If you cannot name anybody, the interest is
still a topic.

Then three rounds, seven minutes each, a new partner every round. Your
partner says your interest back to you in one sentence and you either
accept it or fix it. Then they name who would act on it. Then they name
what you have that the room does not, and one person here you should go and
talk to. They sign every line they write.

Then every card goes on the wall, and you put your initials on any question
you would be glad to work on. Initials mean "I would work on this", not
"this is good".

### Where to look for data

Before assuming data must be bought or scraped: the Cornell library's
licensed holdings, and **Dewey**, a commercial data marketplace the Johnson
College of Business subscribes to and which you can use at no cost. Teams
routinely propose buying data the College already has, or drop a good
question because they assumed the data was unreachable.

**Register at [app.deweydata.io](https://app.deweydata.io) with your
Cornell email**, tonight. Your account sits pending until an administrator
approves it, so do not leave it until you need the data.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.
